newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH MPS DEBATE JARUZELSKI TRIAL FOR MARTIAL LAW.
newsitem.headline: POLISH MPS DEBATE JARUZELSKI TRIAL FOR MARTIAL LAW.

text.p: Poland's parliament on Friday began a final debate on whether former communist leader General Wojciech Jaruzelski should face prosecution for his 1981 declaration of martial law to crush the Solidarity union.

The Constitutional Accountability Commission recommended earlier this year that parliament drop proceedings against Jaruzelski over his clampdown on the first free trade union in the then Soviet bloc, which resulted in the killing of nine protesting miners at the Wujek colliery in south Poland.

The parliamentary Commission, dominated by parties rooted in the old communist system, accepted Jaruzelski's argument that martial law was declared to avert a danger of Soviet military invasion and rescue the country from economic chaos.
But a group of deputies deriving from the former anti-communist opposition submitted a minority motion to put Jaruzelski and other former top communists on trial before a special State Tribunal.

"(As a result of martial law) Poland lost a whole decade. A bad economic situation turned into a catastrophy, many people lost their lives, health, freedom and properties," the deputies wrote justifying the motion.

"Hundreds of thousand of people lost their country, having been forced to emigrate. Lawlessness and lies took over.... Entrusting the case to the State Tribunal would have symbolic significance restoring justice," their statement said.

Parliament is likely to vote in two weeks on whether to prosecute Jaruzelski and is widely expected to drop the case, as the ruling leftist coalition dominated by former communists has held a clear majority since winning 1993 elections.
Jaruzelski, 73, said on Friday he was now more confident than ever that martial law had been justified.
"I am deeply convinced -- today more than 15 years ago, after I read certain documents..., that martial law was at that time a lesser evil," he told private Radio Zet in an interview.
"The country was in chaos, the economy was paralysed and there was a danger of drastic cuts in deliveries of basic commodities (from the Soviet Union) such as oil and gas," Jaruzelski said.
"Besides, there was a military danger with armies of our neighbours gathering around our borders," he added.

Opinion polls show that more than half of Poles think Jaruzelski was justified in imposing martial law -- during which tanks were sent onto the streets and thousands of opposition figures were arrested.

Advocates of Jaruzelski, who was briefly president after the 1989 fall of communism, also praise him for his contribution to the peacful dismantling of the old system during the so-called round-table talks with the opposition.

The parliamentary commission opened the Jaruzelski case five years ago, when groups that had overthown communism were still in power. It reached no conclusion because subsequent parliaments were dissolved ahead of schedule.

Jaruzelski still faces trial in the port city of Gdansk over the shootings by security forces in 1970 of dozens of demonstrators during protests sparked by food price rises. He was defence minister at the time. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
